title: IADT Dental Trauma
description: International Association of Dental Traumatology 2020 guidelines: fractures, luxations, avulsion, primary dentition

workflows.title: Initial dental trauma examination
workflows.overview:
## 1. History

Take a structured trauma history before touching the patient. Cover:

- **When** the injury happened (extra-oral dry time is a treatment-changing variable)
- **Where** and **how** (mechanism, contamination, tetanus risk)
- Loss of consciousness, vomiting, headache (head-injury screen)
- Whether teeth or fragments are unaccounted for
- Tetanus immunisation status
- Medical history, previous dental trauma

## 2. Soft tissue and head exam

- Inspect lips, mucosa, gingiva, frenula for lacerations and embedded fragments
- If fragment is missing and lip/cheek is lacerated, take a soft tissue radiograph to find it
- Refer for medical assessment if head injury features

## 3. Hard tissue and tooth exam

For each injured tooth, record:

1. **Mobility** (normal, increased, none)
2. **Displacement** and direction
3. **Percussion** sound (high metallic = ankylotic; suggests intrusion or lateral luxation)
4. **Tenderness** to percussion or palpation
5. **Visible fractures** (enamel only, enamel-dentin, pulp exposed, sub-gingival)
6. **Pulp sensibility** (cold + EPT) — establishes baseline; transient negative responses are common after luxation

## 4. Radiographs

For maxillary anterior trauma, the standard set is:

1. One **parallel periapical** through the midline (both centrals)
2. One periapical aimed at each lateral incisor
3. One **maxillary occlusal** (best view for lateral luxation, root fracture, alveolar fracture)
4. Periapical of lower incisors

Add **CBCT** when 2D images are inconclusive for root fractures, crown-root fractures, or lateral luxation.

## 5. Photographs

Take clinical photographs at presentation and every follow-up: documents healing, discoloration, infra-occlusion, and provides medico-legal record.

## 6. Diagnosis and combined injuries

Name every injury per tooth: a single tooth may have a crown fracture **and** a luxation. Combined injuries have a worse pulp prognosis. The luxation follow-up schedule overrides the fracture schedule when both are present.

workflows.title: Enamel infraction (permanent tooth)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- **Definition:** incomplete fracture (crack/crazing) of enamel without loss of tooth structure
- Pulp sensibility usually positive
- Normal mobility, no percussion tenderness
- Always check for an associated luxation or root fracture, especially if tender

## 2. Imaging

- One parallel periapical
- No radiographic abnormality expected
- Add views only if other injuries suspected

## 3. Treat

- **Severe infractions:** etch and seal with bonding resin to prevent discoloration and bacterial penetration
- Otherwise: **no treatment**

## 4. Follow up

- **None** if it is genuinely an isolated infraction
- If associated luxation or root fracture, that injury's follow-up schedule prevails

## 5. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** asymptomatic, positive sensibility, continued root development in immature teeth
- **Unfavorable:** symptoms, pulp necrosis/infection, apical periodontitis, arrested root development

workflows.title: Uncomplicated crown fracture (enamel only or enamel-dentin)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Visible loss of enamel +/- dentin
- **No pulp exposure**
- Normal mobility, sensibility usually positive
- Look for associated luxation or root fracture if tender
- If a fragment is missing **and** the lip is lacerated, image the soft tissue

## 2. Imaging

- One parallel periapical
- Soft tissue radiograph if missing fragment + lip laceration

## 3. Treat

### Fragment available

- Soak in water or saline for **20 minutes** to rehydrate, then bond back to the tooth

### Fragment lost

1. **Enamel only:** smooth edges or place composite
2. **Enamel-dentin:** cover exposed dentin with glass ionomer **or** bonding agent + composite
3. **Within 0.5 mm of pulp** (pink, no bleeding): place calcium hydroxide lining, then glass ionomer, then composite

## 4. Follow up

- 6-8 weeks (clinical + radiographic)
- 1 year (clinical + radiographic)
- Use luxation schedule if combined injury

## 5. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** asymptomatic, positive sensibility, intact restoration, continued root development
- **Unfavorable:** symptoms, pulp necrosis and infection, apical periodontitis, arrested root development, lost or breaking restoration

workflows.title: Complicated crown fracture (pulp exposed)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Enamel-dentin fracture **with pulp exposure**
- Exposed pulp sensitive to air, cold, sweets
- Normal mobility unless concomitant luxation

## 2. Imaging

- One parallel periapical
- Soft tissue radiograph if fragment missing + lip laceration

## 3. Treat: preserve the pulp where possible

### Immature teeth (open apex)

- **Highly important to preserve the pulp** for continued root development
- **Partial pulpotomy** (or pulp cap if very small fresh exposure)
- Place **non-setting calcium hydroxide** or **non-staining calcium silicate** on the pulp wound
- Cover with glass ionomer, then restore

### Mature teeth (closed apex)

- **Partial pulpotomy** is still preferred (conservative)
- If a post will be needed for crown retention, then **root canal treatment** instead

### Restoration

- If fragment available: bond back after rehydrating and treating the pulp
- Otherwise: glass ionomer or composite

## 4. Follow up

- 6-8 weeks
- 3 months
- 6 months
- 1 year
- Luxation schedule prevails if combined

## 5. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** asymptomatic, positive sensibility, continued root development, sound restoration
- **Unfavorable:** symptoms, discoloration, pulp necrosis and infection, apical periodontitis, no further root development, failing restoration

workflows.title: Crown-root fracture (permanent tooth)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Fracture involves enamel, dentin, **cementum**
- Typically extends below the gingival margin
- Coronal fragment present and **mobile**
- Tender to percussion
- Determine sub- vs supra-alveolar extent

## 2. Imaging

- One parallel periapical + two more at different angulations
- Maxillary occlusal
- **CBCT** strongly considered to map fracture path, marginal bone relationship, and crown-root ratio

## 3. Emergency stabilisation

- Stabilise the loose fragment to adjacent teeth or to the apical fragment until a definitive plan is made

## 4. Definitive treatment

### Uncomplicated (no pulp exposure)

- Remove coronal fragment, cover dentin with glass ionomer or composite

### Complicated (pulp exposed)

- **Immature root:** partial pulpotomy with non-setting Ca(OH)2 or Ca-silicate; rubber dam isolation
- **Mature root:** pulp removal usually indicated

### Future treatment options

Decide based on age and cooperation:

1. **Orthodontic extrusion** of the apical fragment (may need crown lengthening surgery)
2. **Surgical extrusion**
3. **Root canal treatment** if pulp becomes necrotic, then restore
4. **Root submergence**
5. **Intentional replantation** with or without rotation
6. **Extraction**
7. **Autotransplantation**

## 5. Follow up

- 1 week, 6-8 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 1 year, then yearly for at least **5 years**

## 6. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** asymptomatic, positive sensibility, continued root development, good restoration
- **Unfavorable:** symptoms, discoloration, pulp necrosis, apical periodontitis, marginal bone loss, periodontal inflammation

workflows.title: Root fracture (permanent tooth)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Coronal fragment may be mobile and displaced
- Tender to percussion
- Bleeding from gingival sulcus
- Sensibility may be negative initially (transient)

## 2. Imaging

- Parallel periapical + two angled periapicals + occlusal
- **CBCT** if 2D inconclusive: locates fracture and direction

## 3. Treat

1. **Reposition** the displaced coronal fragment as soon as possible under LA
2. **Verify** position radiographically
3. **Splint** with a passive flexible splint
   - **Apical or mid-third:** 4 weeks
   - **Cervical third:** up to 4 months
4. **Do NOT start root canal treatment** at the emergency visit
5. **Do NOT remove** the coronal fragment, even if cervical, at the emergency visit (cervical root fractures can heal)

## 4. If pulp necrosis develops later

- It usually occurs in the **coronal segment only**
- Endodontic treatment of the coronal segment only
- Apexification approach often needed because length is hard to determine on an oblique fracture
- Apical segment rarely needs treatment

## 5. Mature cervical root fracture, very mobile coronal fragment

- Remove coronal fragment, root canal treat, restore with post-retained crown
- May then need orthodontic extrusion, crown lengthening, or extraction

## 6. Follow up

- 4 weeks (splint removal — apical/mid-third)
- 6-8 weeks
- 4 months (splint removal — cervical third)
- 6 months, 1 year, then yearly for at least **5 years**

## 7. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** signs of repair between fragments, normal/slightly increased mobility, sensibility may return
- **Unfavorable:** extrusion or excessive mobility, radiolucency at fracture line, pulp necrosis with inflammation

workflows.title: Alveolar fracture
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Fracture extends fully from buccal to palatal/lingual cortex
- Whole segment, with several teeth, moves together
- Occlusal disturbance from displacement is common
- Teeth in the segment often do not respond to sensibility tests

## 2. Imaging

- Parallel periapical + two angled views + occlusal
- Panoramic and/or **CBCT** if 2D inconclusive

## 3. Treat

1. **Reposition** the displaced segment under LA
2. **Splint** the teeth with a passive flexible splint for **4 weeks**
3. **Suture** any gingival lacerations
4. **Do NOT start root canal treatment** at the emergency visit
5. **Monitor** pulp condition initially and at follow-ups; endodontics only if necrosis develops

## 4. Follow up

- 4 weeks (splint removal)
- 6-8 weeks
- 4 months
- 6 months
- 1 year
- then yearly for at least **5 years**
- Bone and soft tissue healing are also monitored

## 5. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** sensibility returns, soft tissue healed, radiographic bone repair, slight tenderness at the fracture line may persist
- **Unfavorable:** symptoms, pulp necrosis, apical periodontitis, poor soft tissue healing, non-union, external inflammatory resorption

workflows.title: Concussion (permanent tooth)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Normal mobility
- Tender to percussion and touch
- Pulp sensibility usually positive
- No displacement

## 2. Imaging

- One parallel periapical
- No radiographic abnormality expected

## 3. Treat

- **No active treatment**
- Monitor pulp condition for at least 1 year, preferably longer
- Soft diet, oral hygiene, chlorhexidine 0.12% rinse

## 4. Follow up

- 4 weeks (clinical + radiographic)
- 1 year

## 5. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** asymptomatic, positive sensibility, intact lamina dura, continued root development
- **Unfavorable:** symptoms, pulp necrosis and infection, apical periodontitis, no further root development

workflows.title: Subluxation (permanent tooth)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Tender to touch / light tapping
- **Increased mobility**, but **not displaced**
- Bleeding from gingival crevice possible
- Sensibility may be negative initially (transient)

## 2. Imaging

- Parallel periapical + two angled views + occlusal
- Radiographic appearance usually normal

## 3. Treat

- Normally **no treatment**
- A passive flexible splint for **up to 2 weeks** if excessive mobility or biting tenderness
- Soft diet, chlorhexidine 0.12% rinse

## 4. Follow up

- 2 weeks (splint removal if used)
- 12 weeks
- 6 months
- 1 year

## 5. If external inflammatory resorption appears

- Start root canal treatment immediately
- Calcium hydroxide intra-canal medicament
- Or corticosteroid/antibiotic followed by calcium hydroxide

## 6. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** sensibility returns, intact lamina dura, continued root development
- **Unfavorable:** symptoms, pulp necrosis, apical periodontitis, external inflammatory resorption

workflows.title: Extrusive luxation (permanent tooth)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Tooth appears **elongated**
- Increased mobility
- Likely **no response** to sensibility tests
- Periodontal ligament space widened apically and laterally on radiograph

## 2. Imaging

- Parallel periapical + two angled views + occlusal

## 3. Treat

1. **Reposition** by gently pushing back into the socket under LA
2. **Splint** with passive flexible splint for **2 weeks**
   - Add **4 more weeks** if marginal bone breakdown
3. Monitor pulp condition
4. If pulp becomes necrotic and infected, perform endodontic treatment appropriate to root maturity

## 4. Follow up

- 2 weeks (splint removal)
- 4 weeks
- 8 weeks
- 12 weeks
- 6 months
- 1 year
- yearly for at least **5 years**

## 5. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** asymptomatic, healed periodontium, no marginal bone loss, sensibility may return, continued root development

workflows.title: Intrusive luxation (permanent tooth)
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose

- Tooth driven axially into the alveolar bone
- **Immobile**
- High metallic (ankylotic) percussion sound
- Likely **no response** to sensibility tests
- CEJ visibly more apical than adjacent teeth
- PDL space may be partially or wholly absent on radiograph

## 2. Imaging

- Parallel periapical + two angled views + occlusal

## 3. Treat by root maturity and intrusion depth

### Immature root (open apex)

- **Allow re-eruption** without intervention, regardless of depth
- If no movement within **4 weeks**, initiate **orthodontic** repositioning
- Spontaneous pulp revascularization is possible — root canal treatment only if necrosis/inflammatory resorption

### Mature root (closed apex)

1. **Intrusion < 3 mm:** allow re-eruption. If none within 8 weeks, **surgically reposition** and splint 4 weeks (or orthodontic before ankylosis)
2. **Intrusion 3-7 mm:** **surgical** (preferred) or orthodontic repositioning
3. **Intrusion > 7 mm:** **surgical** repositioning
4. Pulp almost always becomes necrotic — start **root canal treatment at 2 weeks** or as soon as access allows, with corticosteroid/antibiotic or calcium hydroxide

## 4. Follow up

- 2 weeks
- 4 weeks (splint removal)
- 8 weeks
- 12 weeks
- 6 months
- 1 year
- yearly for at least **5 years**

## 5. Outcome flags

- **Favorable:** tooth in place or re-erupting, intact lamina dura, no resorption, continued root development
- **Unfavorable:** ankylotic, pulp necrosis, apical periodontitis, replacement or inflammatory resorption

workflows.title: Avulsed permanent tooth: first aid at the scene
workflows.overview:
## 1. Confirm it is a permanent tooth

- **Primary teeth must NOT be replanted**

## 2. Calm the patient

## 3. Find and pick up the tooth

- Hold by the **crown only** (white part)
- Do NOT touch the root

## 4. If dirty, rinse briefly

- Milk, saline, or saliva
- 10 seconds maximum, no scrubbing

## 5. Replant immediately if possible

- Replantation at the scene is the best treatment
- Once back in the socket, the patient bites on gauze, handkerchief or napkin to hold it

## 6. If replantation is not possible, store the tooth

In descending order of preference:

1. **Milk**
2. **HBSS** (Hank's Balanced Salt Solution / Save-a-Tooth)
3. **Saliva** (spit into a glass)
4. **Saline**
5. **Water** (poor, but better than air-drying)

Do this within minutes. Dry root surfaces lose PDL viability rapidly.

## 7. Get to a dentist

- Bring tooth and patient to the dental clinic immediately
- Tetanus status will need checking

workflows.title: Avulsion management: closed apex permanent tooth
workflows.overview:
## 1. Triage by extra-oral conditions (PDL viability)

1. **Replanted at scene** (immediate / very short time): PDL cells most likely viable
2. **Stored in physiologic medium or dry < 60 min:** PDL cells may be viable but compromised
3. **Dry > 60 min:** PDL cells likely non-viable

## 2. Replant

### Already replanted at scene
- Clean area; verify position clinically and radiographically
- Reposition only if malpositioned (digital pressure; may go up to 48 h)
- LA preferably without vasoconstrictor

### Stored / dry < 60 min
1. Rinse root surface with saline or balanced solution
2. Tooth in storage medium while history/exam taken
3. LA without vasoconstrictor
4. Irrigate socket with saline; reposition any wall fragment
5. Replant slowly with **slight digital pressure** (no excessive force)
6. Verify position clinically and radiographically

### Dry > 60 min (delayed)
1. Remove debris by agitation in physiologic medium
2. LA, irrigate socket, replant slowly
3. Counsel: PDL is dead → expect ankylosis-related (replacement) resorption
4. Replantation still preferred over loss for maintaining alveolar bone and keeping options open

## 3. Stabilise (all groups)

- **Passive, flexible splint for 2 weeks**
- Stainless steel wire ≤ 0.4 mm or nylon fishing line 0.13-0.25 mm bonded to teeth
- Composite kept off the gingiva and proximal areas
- **4 weeks** if associated alveolar/jaw fracture
- Suture gingival lacerations

## 4. Endodontic plan (closed apex always needs RCT)

- **Initiate RCT within 2 weeks** of replantation, before splint removal
- Calcium hydroxide intra-canal medicament for up to 1 month, then obturate
- Or corticosteroid/antibiotic medicament placed immediately, left at least 6 weeks

## 5. Adjuncts

- **Systemic antibiotics:** amoxicillin/penicillin (or doxycycline if ≥ 12 y) — first choice
- **Tetanus:** refer for booster review
- **Patient instructions:** soft diet 2 weeks, soft brush after meals, chlorhexidine 0.12% twice daily 2 weeks, no contact sports

## 6. Follow up

- 2 weeks (splint removal)
- 4 weeks
- 3 months
- 6 months
- 1 year
- yearly for at least **5 years**

## 7. Outcomes

- **Favorable:** asymptomatic, normal mobility/percussion, no radiolucency, no resorption, normal lamina dura
- **Unfavorable:** ankylotic percussion, infection-related (inflammatory) or ankylosis-related (replacement) resorption, infra-positioning in growing patients

workflows.title: Primary tooth luxation: extrusion, lateral, intrusion
workflows.overview:
## 1. General principles for primary teeth

- The driver of treatment is **protecting the underlying permanent tooth germ**
- Pulp sensibility tests are unreliable in primary teeth and **not recommended**
- Spontaneous re-eruption and repositioning are common
- **Observation is often the right answer** if airway, occlusion, and aspiration risk are safe
- Avoid extractions where possible (dental anxiety risk)
- Refer to a child-oriented team for complex injuries

## 2. Extrusive luxation

- **No occlusal interference:** let it spontaneously reposition
- **Excessively mobile or extruded > 3 mm:** **extract** under LA

## 3. Lateral luxation

- **Minimal/no occlusal interference:** allow spontaneous repositioning (usually within 6 months)
- **Severe displacement, two options:**
  1. **Extract** (if risk of ingestion or aspiration)
  2. Gently reposition; if unstable, splint 4 weeks with flexible splint

## 4. Intrusive luxation

- **Allow spontaneous re-eruption** regardless of direction of displacement
- Improvement usually within 6 months, sometimes up to 1 year
- Rapid referral (within days) to a child-oriented team
- Previous advice to extract if root pointed at the germ is **no longer recommended** — extraction itself can damage the germ and there is good evidence of spontaneous re-eruption

## 5. Avulsion

- **Do NOT replant** an avulsed primary tooth (replantation burden + germ damage + aspiration risk)
- Confirm tooth is accounted for; if missing, a radiograph is essential to rule out intrusion

## 6. Common adjuncts

- Soft brush + alcohol-free chlorhexidine 0.1-0.2% twice daily for 1 week
- Soft diet, careful eating
- Analgesia (ibuprofen / paracetamol) for pain
- Inform parents about possible permanent-tooth disturbances
- Tetanus booster if environmental contamination

## 7. Follow-up themes

- Clinical reviews 1 week, 6-8 weeks, 6 months, 1 year (varies by injury)
- Radiographs only when clinical findings suggest pathology
- Further review at age 6 to monitor permanent tooth eruption (especially after intrusion, avulsion, alveolar fracture)

workflows.title: Primary tooth crown fractures and crown-root fractures
workflows.overview:
## 1. Enamel fracture

- **No radiograph** needed
- **Smooth sharp edges**
- Parental education: gentle eating, soft brush + alcohol-free chlorhexidine
- **No follow up** required

## 2. Enamel-dentin fracture (no pulp exposure)

- Baseline radiograph optional; **soft tissue radiograph** if fragment missing and lip lacerated
- **Cover exposed dentin** with glass ionomer or composite
- Restore now or at a later visit
- Clinical follow up at **6-8 weeks**; radiograph only if signs of pathology

## 3. Complicated crown fracture (pulp exposed)

- Periapical or occlusal radiograph at presentation
- **Partial pulpotomy** under LA: non-setting calcium hydroxide on pulp wound, then glass ionomer, then composite
- **Cervical pulpotomy** if exposure is large
- *Or* no treatment in the emergency window if rapid referral (within days) to a child-oriented team is possible
- Follow up: **1 week, 6-8 weeks, 1 year** (radiograph at 1 year)

## 4. Crown-root fracture

- Periapical or occlusal radiograph at presentation
- Often best managed with **no treatment in emergency** if rapid referral possible
- If treating now, remove the loose fragment and decide if crown is restorable:
  - **Restorable, pulp not exposed:** cover dentin with glass ionomer
  - **Restorable, pulp exposed:** pulpotomy or RCT depending on root development
  - **Unrestorable:** extract loose fragments carefully (avoid permanent germ); leave any firm root fragment in situ, or extract whole tooth
- Follow up: **1 week, 6-8 weeks, 1 year**

## 5. Throughout

- Manage with a child-oriented team where possible
- Discoloration after trauma is common, often transient; **do not treat discoloration alone** without infection signs
- Educate parents on signs of pulp infection: sinus tract, swelling, abscess, increased mobility, persistent dark gray discoloration

workflows.title: Primary tooth root fracture and alveolar fracture
workflows.overview:
## 1. Diagnose root fracture

- Coronal fragment may be mobile and displaced
- Occlusal interference possible
- Fracture usually **mid-root or apical third**
- Periapical or occlusal radiograph at presentation

## 2. Treat root fracture

1. **Coronal fragment not displaced:** no treatment
2. **Displaced, not excessively mobile:** leave to spontaneously reposition, even with mild occlusal interference
3. **Displaced, excessively mobile, occlusal interference:** two options under LA
   - **A.** Extract only the coronal fragment; leave apical fragment to resorb
   - **B.** Reposition gently; if unstable, splint to adjacent uninjured teeth for 4 weeks

## 3. Follow up: root fracture

- Not displaced: 1 week, 6-8 weeks, 1 year, then yearly until permanent eruption
- Repositioned and splinted: 1 week, 4 weeks (splint removal), 8 weeks, 1 year
- Coronal fragment extracted: 1 year

## 4. Diagnose alveolar fracture

- Several teeth move as one segment
- Occlusal interference usual
- Periapical/occlusal radiograph; lateral view useful for labial displacement

## 5. Treat alveolar fracture

1. **Reposition** displaced segment under LA if mobile or occluding
2. **Splint** with flexible splint to adjacent uninjured teeth for **4 weeks**
3. Done by a child-oriented team

## 6. Follow up: alveolar fracture

- 1 week, 4 weeks (splint removal), 8 weeks, 1 year
- Further review at age 6 to monitor permanent tooth eruption
- Radiographic review at 4 weeks and 1 year (assesses germ position)

## 7. Throughout

- Consider analgesia (ibuprofen, paracetamol) — these injuries can be painful
- Soft brush + alcohol-free chlorhexidine 0.1-0.2% twice daily for 1 week
- Tetanus booster if environmental contamination

firstPrinciples.title: PDL viability is the master variable in avulsion prognosis
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: An avulsed permanent tooth lives or dies by the cells on its root surface. Time and storage medium decide whether those cells survive long enough to reattach.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The cells that matter

The periodontal ligament holds the tooth in bone through a thin layer of viable cells on the root surface. When the tooth is ripped out, those cells are still alive but exposed. They tolerate brief mechanical insult. They do not tolerate drying or osmotic shock. After about 30 minutes of dry time most are dead, and after 60 minutes essentially all are dead [1].

## Why it changes everything at the chair

If the PDL cells are alive, replantation can heal with a normal periodontium. If they are dead, the body removes the root and replaces it with bone (replacement resorption / ankylosis). The tooth gets stiff, loses its protective ligament, and infra-occludes as the rest of the face grows. So three things drive treatment: extra-oral time, the storage medium, and how the tooth was handled. The clinician's job at the scene and on arrival is to keep those cells alive — picking up by the crown, never the root, milk over water over air [2].

## What this means for protocols

The IADT triage of avulsed teeth into 'replanted at scene', 'under 60 minutes with medium', and 'over 60 minutes' is a direct expression of PDL viability. Even with dead PDL, replantation is still done to preserve alveolar bone and keep options open, but the patient is told in advance the long-term prognosis is poor [3].

citations.quote: After an extra-alveolar dry time of 30 minutes, most PDL cells are non-viable.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, Section 3

citations.quote: In descending order of preference, milk, HBSS, saliva (after spitting into a glass for instance), or saline are suitable and convenient storage mediums. Although water is a poor medium, it is better than leaving the tooth to air-dry.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, Section 2 (First Aid)

citations.quote: Delayed replantation has a poor long-term prognosis. The periodontal ligament becomes necrotic and is not expected to regenerate. The expected outcome is ankylosis-related (replacement) root resorption.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, Section 3.1.3

firstPrinciples.title: An immature pulp can heal in ways an adult pulp cannot
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Open-apex teeth have a wide blood supply at the apex and undifferentiated cells inside. They can revascularise, redevelop, and survive trauma that would kill a mature pulp.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why immaturity helps

A tooth with an open apex has a wide foramen and a pulp packed with progenitor cells. After luxation or even avulsion, capillaries can regrow into the canal and re-establish a blood supply. After traumatic pulp exposure, the pulp can be capped or partially removed and the rest will keep working and finish forming the root [1].

## Why this is the basis for 'wait and see'

This is why open-apex teeth are managed conservatively. Routine root canal treatment after avulsion or luxation is not initiated in immature teeth — the goal is spontaneous revascularisation [2]. After a complicated crown fracture, partial pulpotomy is preferred over pulpectomy [3]. Endodontic intervention is held back until clinical or radiographic signs of necrosis or infection-related resorption appear.

## The trade-off and why follow-up is intense

The price of waiting is that infection-related (inflammatory) resorption proceeds rapidly in children, and a tooth and its supporting bone can be lost quickly if it is missed [2]. So immature teeth are reviewed more frequently than mature ones.

citations.quote: The immature permanent tooth has considerable capacity for healing after traumatic pulp exposure, luxation injury, or root fracture.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: General Introduction, Section 2.2

citations.quote: In teeth with open apices, spontaneous pulp space revascularization may occur. Thus, root canal treatment should be avoided unless there is clinical or radiographic evidence of pulp necrosis and infection of the root canal system on follow-up examinations. The risk of infection-related (inflammatory) root resorption should be weighed against the chances of obtaining pulp space revascularization. Such resorption is very rapid in children.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, Section 10

citations.quote: In patients where teeth have immature roots and open apices, it is very important to preserve the pulp. Partial pulpotomy or pulp capping are recommended in order to promote further root development.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Table 4

firstPrinciples.title: Sensibility tests measure nerves, not blood supply
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: A negative cold or EPT response after trauma does not mean the pulp is dead. Many traumatised pulps lose neural function transiently while staying alive.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What the test actually does

The cold test and the electric pulp test rely on A-delta nerve fibres in the pulp. A positive response means those nerves are conducting. Vitality, in contrast, is whether the pulp has a blood supply. The two are not the same thing [1].

## Why it matters at the chair

After luxation, neural conduction can shut down for weeks or months while the pulp is still alive. So a single negative response after trauma is not a license to start root canal treatment [1]. The IADT explicitly says endodontic treatment should not be initiated solely on the basis of no response to pulp sensibility testing [2].

## What you do instead

Testing is still done at every appointment, but as a baseline and a trend. The diagnosis of pulp necrosis comes from the combination of multiple negative tests over time, plus radiographic signs (periapical radiolucency, infection-related resorption), plus clinical signs (sinus tract, swelling, persistent grey-black discoloration with infection). Pulse oximetry and laser Doppler measure actual flow but are not yet routine clinical tools.

citations.quote: It is important to understand that sensibility testing assesses neural activity and not vascular supply. Thus, this testing might be unreliable due to a transient lack of neural response or undifferentiation of A-delta nerve fibers in young teeth. The temporary loss of sensibility is a frequent finding during post-traumatic pulp healing, especially after luxation injuries.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Section 5.1

citations.quote: Positive response to pulp sensibility testing; however, a false negative response is possible for several months. Endodontic treatment should not be started solely on the basis of no response to pulp sensibility testing.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Table 9 (Concussion)

firstPrinciples.title: The primary tooth apex sits on top of the permanent germ
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Treatment decisions in the primary dentition are dominated by the developing permanent tooth above it, not by the primary tooth itself.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The anatomy that drives everything

The roots of primary incisors lie immediately labial to or directly over the permanent tooth germs. Any force, instrument or extraction near a primary apex transmits to the germ above [1]. This is why management of primary trauma differs so radically from permanent-tooth management.

## Where this changes the protocol

Intruded primary teeth are no longer extracted prophylactically just because the root is pointing at the germ — extraction itself can damage the germ, and there is good evidence that intruded primary teeth re-erupt spontaneously [2]. Avulsed primary teeth are not replanted at all (replantation pushes the root back through the same anatomy that traumatised the germ in the first place) [3]. Pulpotomies, splints and endodontics are weighed against the alternative of leaving the tooth alone if it does not threaten airway, occlusion, or comfort.

## The long shadow

Parents must be told that even with optimal management the permanent successor can still come through with enamel hypoplasia, malformation, eruption disturbance, or impaction. This is more common after intrusion, avulsion and alveolar fracture.

citations.quote: There is a close spatial relationship between the apex of the primary tooth root and the underlying permanent tooth germ. Tooth malformation, impacted teeth, and eruption disturbances in the developing permanent dentition are some of the consequences that can occur following injuries to primary teeth and the alveolar bone.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Primary Dentition, Section 1.8

citations.quote: For intrusive and lateral luxation injuries, previous Guidelines have recommended the immediate extraction of the traumatized primary tooth if the direction of displacement of the root is toward the permanent tooth germ. This action is no longer advised due to (a) evidence of spontaneous re-eruption for intruded primary teeth, (b) the concern that further damage may be inflicted on the tooth germ during extraction, and (c) the lack of evidence that immediate extraction will minimize further damage to the permanent tooth germ.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Primary Dentition, Section 1.8

citations.quote: An avulsed primary tooth should not be replanted. Reasons include a significant treatment burden (including replantation, splint placement and removal, root canal treatment) for a young child as well as the potential of causing further damage to the permanent tooth or to its eruption.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Primary Dentition, Section 1.10

firstPrinciples.title: Splints should be flexible, not rigid
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The PDL needs slight movement to heal. Rigid splints stiffen the tooth and promote ankylosis. Flexible splints stabilise without immobilising.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why physiological motion helps

Replanted and luxated teeth heal best when the tooth is held in position but allowed slight functional movement. This stimulates PDL fibroblasts to lay down new attachment fibres and reduces the risk of ankylosis. Animal studies show more than 60% of the PDL's mechanical properties return within two weeks of injury when the tooth is allowed gentle function [1].

## What that looks like clinically

The IADT recommends a passive flexible splint for almost every injury that needs splinting: stainless steel wire up to 0.4 mm, or nylon fishing line 0.13-0.25 mm, bonded with composite [2]. The composite is kept off the gingiva and out of interproximal areas to prevent plaque retention. The splint is placed labially so it does not interfere with occlusion or block palatal endodontic access.

## Duration matches injury, not preference

Most injuries get 2 weeks (subluxation if needed, extrusion, avulsion). Lateral luxation and intrusion get 4 weeks. Cervical-third root fractures get up to 4 months because the coronal fragment is unstable. Beyond those durations, the splint stops helping and starts harming.

citations.quote: An animal study has shown that more than 60% of the mechanical properties of the injured PDL return within 2 weeks following injury.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, Section 8

citations.quote: Current evidence supports short-term, passive, and flexible splints for splinting of luxated, avulsed, and root-fractured teeth. When using wire-composite splints, physiological stabilization can be obtained with stainless steel wire up to 0.4 mm in diameter.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Section 6

firstPrinciples.title: Mature avulsed teeth always need root canal treatment within 2 weeks
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: A closed-apex tooth has no chance of pulp revascularisation after avulsion. Without endodontic treatment, the necrotic pulp drives infection-related resorption.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why mature pulps cannot heal

A closed-apex tooth has only a tiny apical foramen. After avulsion, it cannot be re-vascularised — the blood supply cannot grow back through that constriction in time. The pulp dies and bacteria from dentinal tubules colonise the necrotic tissue [1]. Toxins diffuse out through the dentin and trigger osteoclasts on the root surface. The result is infection-related (inflammatory) external resorption, which can destroy the root within weeks.

## What the protocol does about it

The IADT mandates that root canal treatment of a closed-apex avulsed tooth is initiated within 2 weeks of replantation, before splint removal [1]. The intra-canal medicament is calcium hydroxide for up to 1 month before obturation, or alternatively a corticosteroid/antibiotic placed immediately and left for 6 weeks. Either keeps the pulp space sterile and disrupts the resorptive cascade.

## Why this is different from open-apex avulsion

In an immature tooth the wide apex still allows revascularisation, so RCT is held back. In a mature tooth there is no such option, and waiting only loses the tooth.

citations.quote: When endodontic treatment is indicated (teeth with closed apex), treatment should be initiated within 2 weeks post-replantation. Calcium hydroxide is recommended as an intracanal medicament for up to 1 month followed by root canal filling. If a corticosteroid or corticosteroid/antibiotic mixture is chosen to be used as an anti-inflammatory and anti-resorptive intracanal medicament, it should be placed immediately or shortly after replantation and left in situ for at least 6 weeks.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, Section 10

firstPrinciples.title: Replant even when the prognosis is poor
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Even an avulsed tooth with dead PDL is replanted, because not replanting is irreversible and replantation preserves the alveolus and future treatment options.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The reasoning

If the PDL is dead, replantation will end in ankylosis and replacement resorption. The tooth will eventually be lost. So why replant? Because removing the tooth permanently is a one-way decision and replantation keeps every option open [1]. The replanted tooth, even ankylosed, holds the alveolar ridge while the patient grows and the family decides between decoronation, autotransplantation, bridge, denture or implant.

## What the patient needs to hear

The parent of a child with a dry-time-over-60-minutes avulsion is told the tooth will probably be lost in time, that ankylosis and infra-position are likely, and that decoronation may be needed before facial growth completes [1]. They are not told the tooth will definitely survive. But they are told that replanting now is almost always the right decision, because extraction can be done later if needed.

## The exceptions

IADT lists genuine reasons not to replant: severe caries or periodontal disease in the avulsed tooth, severe immunocompromise, severe cardiac conditions, an uncooperative patient or one needing sedation. These are individual decisions and rare.

citations.quote: Therefore, the decision to replant a permanent tooth is almost always the correct decision even if the extra-oral dry time is more than 60 minutes. Replantation will keep future treatment options open. The tooth can always be extracted, if needed, and at the appropriate point following prompt inter-disciplinary assessment.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, Section 3.1.3

firstPrinciples.title: Combined injuries are worse than the sum of their parts
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: A crown fracture plus a luxation injury has a much higher rate of pulp necrosis than either alone. The follow-up schedule reflects the worst injury, not the average.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The synergy

When a tooth has both a crown fracture and a luxation, the crown fracture opens the pulp to bacteria from the dentinal tubules at the same time as the luxation has cut its blood supply [1]. The pulp's ability to defend itself depends on staying perfused, and a luxated pulp cannot. Studies show concurrent crown fractures significantly increase the risk of pulp necrosis and infection in concussed and subluxated teeth, and even more so in laterally luxated teeth [2].

## What changes in management

The immediate management of each injury is unchanged — you still treat the fracture and reposition the tooth. What changes is the follow-up schedule and the threshold for endodontic intervention. The IADT rule is that the more frequent luxation schedule prevails over the less frequent fracture schedule [3]. Mature teeth with severe combined injuries may justify preventive endodontic treatment before symptoms appear.

## Why this matters

Missing pulp necrosis in a combined injury is the single biggest avoidable cause of late tooth loss after dental trauma. Frequent reviews with sensibility testing, radiographs and photographs catch it before resorption gets out of hand.

citations.quote: The combination of two different types of injuries occurring concurrently to the same tooth will be more detrimental than a single injury, creating a negative synergistic effect.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Section 2

citations.quote: Concurrent crown fractures significantly increase the risk of pulp necrosis and infection in teeth with concussion or subluxation injuries and mature root development. Similarly, crown fractures with or without pulp exposure significantly increase the risk of pulp necrosis and infection in teeth with lateral luxation.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Section 2

citations.quote: Since prognosis is worse in combined injuries, the more frequent follow-up regimen for luxation injuries prevails over the less frequent regime for fractures.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Section 11

firstPrinciples.title: Cervical root fractures heal more slowly because the coronal fragment is more mobile
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Splint duration after a root fracture is determined by where on the root the fracture sits. Cervical fractures need four months, mid-root and apical fractures need four weeks.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The mechanics

When a root fracture heals, callus forms across the fracture line. That callus needs immobility to organise. The closer the fracture is to the cervical margin, the longer the lever arm of the coronal fragment and the more it moves under occlusal load [1]. A cervical fracture sees more force per unit time than an apical one, so it needs a longer splinting period to allow the same healing.

## What that looks like clinically

Apical-third and mid-root fractures are splinted for 4 weeks. Cervical-third fractures are splinted for up to 4 months [1]. The clinician verifies position, applies a passive flexible splint, and resists the temptation to remove a cervical fragment that looks unstable: cervical root fractures can heal, and removing the fragment commits the patient to a post-and-core or extraction.

## When it does not heal

If the coronal fragment becomes excessively mobile, infection appears, or the radiograph shows progressive radiolucency at the fracture line, the pulp has likely become necrotic in the coronal fragment. RCT is then performed on that segment only — the apical segment rarely needs treatment.

citations.quote: Stabilize the mobile coronal segment with a passive and flexible splint for 4 wk. If the fracture is located cervically, stabilization for a longer period of time (up to 4 mo) may be needed. Cervical fractures have the potential to heal. Thus, the coronal fragment, especially if not mobile, should not be removed at the emergency visit.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Table 7 (Root fracture)

firstPrinciples.title: Pulp canal obliteration is healing, not pathology
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: After luxation in an open-apex tooth, the canal often fills in with hard tissue. This is the pulp's response to injury, not a sign that endodontic treatment is needed.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What is happening biologically

When an immature tooth survives a severe luxation or root fracture, surviving odontoblasts and pulp progenitors lay down hard tissue inside the canal as part of repair. Over months to a couple of years the canal narrows and may obliterate radiographically. This indicates that there is viable tissue in the canal — exactly what the open-apex protocol is hoping for [1].

## Why it matters at the chair

A radiograph showing canal obliteration after luxation can look alarming, but it is a favourable outcome. The IADT lists pulp canal obliteration as the expected mechanism by which the pulp heals after replantation in immature avulsed teeth [2]. Endodontic treatment is not initiated because of obliteration alone — only signs of necrosis or infection (sinus tract, periapical radiolucency, persistent symptoms) justify intervention.

## Where it shows up

Obliteration is most common after extrusion, intrusion, lateral luxation, and root fractures. It is less common after subluxation and crown fracture. Knowing this lets the clinician reassure parents and avoid pre-emptive RCT on a tooth that is healing.

citations.quote: Pulp canal obliteration (PCO) occurs more frequently in teeth with open apices which have suffered a severe luxation injury. It usually indicates the presence of viable tissue within the root canal. Extrusion, intrusion, and lateral luxation injuries have high rates of PCO.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Section 12

citations.quote: Pulp canal obliteration is expected and can be recognized radiographically sometime during the first year after the trauma. It is considered to be the mechanism by which the 'pulp' heals after replantation of avulsed immature permanent teeth.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Avulsion of Permanent Teeth, Section 11.2.2

firstPrinciples.title: First aid at the scene determines the outcome of avulsion
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Most of the prognosis of an avulsed tooth is decided in the first 15 minutes by laypeople who are not dentists. Public education and clear advice by phone are part of dental practice.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why this is unique among emergencies

Avulsion is one of the few real emergencies in dentistry where what happens before the patient reaches the surgery dictates the long-term outcome [1]. By the time the child arrives at the clinic, PDL viability is already largely set. The dentist's clinical work is good, but it cannot recover dead PDL cells.

## What this means for practice

Dentists are expected to provide first-aid advice to teachers, parents, paramedics and the public, by phone if needed: confirm permanent tooth, hold by the crown, brief milk rinse if dirty, replant immediately, bite on gauze. If replantation at the scene is impossible, store in milk (or HBSS, saliva, saline) and bring the patient and the tooth to the clinic immediately. Posters such as 'Save a Tooth' and apps such as ToothSOS are part of this education effort.

## The variables to control

The modifiable variables are dry time and storage medium. Both are decided by the first person on scene. Dental teams who train sports coaches and school first-aid staff buy themselves better outcomes for patients they will never meet at the moment of injury.

citations.quote: The prognosis for avulsed permanent teeth is heavily dependent on the actions taken at the place of accident. Promotion of public awareness of first-aid treatment for the avulsed tooth is strongly encouraged. Treatment choices and prognosis for the avulsed tooth are largely dependent on the viability of the periodontal ligament (PDL), and the maturity of the root.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: General Introduction, Section 2.3

firstPrinciples.title: Lateral luxation looks immobile because the apex is locked in bone
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: A laterally luxated tooth feels stuck not because it healed quickly but because the apex has been driven into the cortical plate. Repositioning has to disengage it before it will move.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What is actually happening

In lateral luxation, the crown is pushed in one direction (usually palatal) and the apex is forced in the opposite direction through the buccal (or lingual) cortical plate. The bone fractures and grips the apex. Clinically the tooth is paradoxically rigid and gives a high metallic 'ankylotic' percussion sound [1].

## Why the repositioning technique matters

If you push the crown back into the socket without first freeing the apex, you levering the apex against intact bone and tear more PDL. The IADT technique is to palpate the gingiva and feel where the apex is, then use one finger to push downwards over the apex (releasing it from its bone trap) while another finger pushes the crown back into place [1].

## Splint and endodontic implications

Lateral luxation tears PDL on a wider area than extrusion or subluxation, so it is splinted for 4 weeks rather than 2. Mature teeth almost always lose the pulp because the apical neurovascular bundle is severed; RCT is started at about 2 weeks, with corticosteroid/antibiotic or calcium hydroxide medicament to prevent inflammatory resorption. Immature teeth may revascularise and are watched.

citations.quote: The tooth is frequently immobile as the apex of the root is 'locked' in by the bone fracture. Percussion will give a high metallic (ankylotic) sound. Reposition the tooth digitally by disengaging it from its locked position and gently reposition it into its original location under local anesthesia. Method: Palpate the gingiva to feel the apex of the tooth. Use one finger to push downwards over the apical end of the tooth, then use another finger or thumb to push the tooth back into its socket.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Table 12 (Lateral luxation)

firstPrinciples.title: External inflammatory resorption is bacterial, not mechanical
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Resorption around a traumatised root is driven by bacteria inside the canal, not by the original injury. Removing the bacteria with calcium hydroxide stops the process.
firstPrinciples.body:
## How it gets started

After trauma, dentinal tubules give bacteria a path from the pulp to the root surface. Bacterial toxins diffuse out and activate osteoclast-like cells on the cementum. Those cells eat both root and the adjacent bone, producing radiolucencies on both sides of the fracture line. Without intervention, resorption can destroy a root in weeks, especially in children.

## Why calcium hydroxide stops it

Calcium hydroxide is strongly alkaline. Inside a root canal it raises tubule pH, kills bacteria, and removes the chemical signal that drives the osteoclasts. The IADT protocol is to start root canal treatment as soon as inflammatory resorption is detected, dress with calcium hydroxide for 3 weeks, replace every 3 months, and continue until the radiolucencies disappear and bone repair is visible. Final obturation comes only after bone repair [1].

## When to act

In any traumatised tooth, the appearance of progressive radiolucency along the root or in the bone immediately adjacent to it is interpreted as inflammatory resorption until proven otherwise. There is no justification for waiting, especially in children where the process moves fast.

citations.quote: Whenever there is evidence of infection-related (inflammatory) external resorption, root canal treatment should be initiated immediately. The canal should be medicated with calcium hydroxide. The calcium hydroxide should be placed for 3 weeks and replaced every 3 months until the radiolucencies of the resorptive lesions disappear. Final obturation of the root canal can be performed when bone repair is visible radiographically.
citations.source: IADT Guidelines 2020: Fractures and Luxations, Section 13.3
